posts.title: Continent on admission, leaking at discharge
posts.insight: In one hospital study, about 1 in 6 continent people aged 70 and over said at discharge they could no longer control their bladder, and pad or catheter use was linked with this. Help to the toilet should be the default for people who were continent before admission.
posts.angle: Challenges pads and catheters as the default for continent older inpatients, while stating that the study shows a link and that frailer people are more likely to be given pads.
posts.position_basis: mixed: the 1 in 6 figure and the pad and catheter link are empirical (association); the CDC statement is guidance; 'help to the toilet should be the default' is clinical and ethical judgement

captions.x:
In an Israeli hospital study, 352 people aged 70 and over were admitted to a medical ward able to control their bladder. At discharge, about 1 in 6 (60 people) said they no longer could.

People who wore pads or had a catheter for most of the stay were more likely to report new leaking than people who used the toilet themselves, even after allowing for age, illness severity, mobility and memory.

This is a link, not proof that pads caused it. Frailer people are more likely to be given pads, and no observational study fully removes that.

US infection control guidance (CDC) lists a catheter used as a substitute for nursing care of incontinence as an inappropriate use.

We should make help to the toilet the default for anyone who was continent before admission. A new "incontinent" entry in the notes should prompt one question: were they continent last week?
captions.linkedin:
In an Israeli hospital study, 352 people aged 70 and over were admitted to a medical ward, all able to control their bladder beforehand. At discharge, about 1 in 6 (60 people) said they could no longer control it.

The researchers asked how each person had managed their bladder during the stay. People who wore pads or had a catheter for most of it were more likely to report new leaking than people who used the toilet themselves. This held after allowing for age, illness severity, mobility and memory. The adjusted odds ratios were about 2.6 for pads and 4.3 for catheters, with wide confidence intervals (catheters 1.5 to 11.8).

Three limits apply. It was one hospital, in one country. Leaking was self-reported at discharge and not followed afterwards, so we do not know how many people recovered. And the study shows a link, not that pads caused the leaking: a Danish study of about 2,000 older patients found frailer people are more likely to be given pads, and no observational study can fully remove that.

The guidance on catheters is clearer. US infection control guidance (CDC, 2009) says catheters should not be used to manage incontinence, and lists using one "as a substitute for nursing care" as an inappropriate use.

My position: for a person who was continent before admission, help to the toilet should be the default, with call bells answered and walking aids within reach. A pad may still be the right choice for some people, after someone has asked.

When the notes say "incontinent, pad in situ", ask: were they continent last week?
captions.bluesky:
In an Israeli study of 352 people aged 70+ who were continent on admission, about 1 in 6 said at discharge they could no longer control their bladder. Pads or catheters for most of the stay were linked with this; frailty may explain part of the link.

We should make help to the toilet the default.

posts.title: Cranberry: it depends who you are
posts.insight: The 2023 Cochrane review found cranberry products probably cut repeat infections a little in women who keep getting them, but did not show a clear benefit for older people living in care homes or other institutions.
posts.angle: Who was studied decides who a result applies to; the same product has a different verdict in different groups.
posts.position_basis: empirical finding (Cochrane review figures) plus clinical interpretation (who to discuss it with)

captions.x:
Cranberry products for urine infections: the evidence gives a different answer depending on who you are.

The largest review (Cochrane, 2023) pooled 50 trials with 8,857 people.

For women who keep getting urine infections, cranberry probably helps a little. In the trials, about 18 in 100 women taking cranberry had an infection, against about 24 in 100 without it.

For older people living in care homes or other institutions, the trials did not show a clear benefit. About 11 in 100 had an infection either way. Only 3 trials studied this group, so the result is uncertain.

If you keep getting infections, cranberry is a reasonable thing to discuss. If a care home suggests cranberry juice to prevent infections, ask what else is being done.
captions.linkedin:
Cranberry products for urine infections: the evidence gives a different answer depending on who you are.

The largest review of the question (Cochrane, 2023) pooled 50 trials with 8,857 people. Its results split by group.

1. Women who keep getting urine infections. Cranberry probably helps a little. About 18 in 100 women taking cranberry had an infection during the trials, compared with about 24 in 100 without it. The range of plausible results runs from about 13 to 24 in 100, so the benefit could be small.

2. Children, and people prone to infection after a bladder procedure. Cranberry probably reduces infections in these groups too.

3. Older people living in care homes or other institutions. The trials did not show a clear benefit. About 11 in 100 had an infection with or without cranberry. Only 3 trials studied this group, and the result fits anything from about 4 fewer to about 3 more infections per 100 people.

Stomach side effects were probably no more common than with a dummy product.

The reading lesson: a finding in one group does not transfer to another. Women with repeated infections are a different population from frail residents of care homes.

For a woman who keeps getting infections, cranberry is a reasonable option to discuss. For an older person in a care home, the evidence does not support relying on it. If a home suggests cranberry juice, ask what else is in the plan.

posts.title: Smell and colour are poor guides
posts.insight: Smelly or dark urine on its own is a poor guide to infection in older people; new urinary symptoms, fever or visible blood are what to report.
posts.angle: Corrects a named, common belief with honest nuance: a change in the urine raises the chance of lab signs a little, but those signs are common without infection.
posts.position_basis: mixed: study figures are empirical; 'nobody should be given antibiotics for smell or colour alone' is clinical judgement

captions.x:
Many people, including care staff, take smelly or dark urine as a sign of infection. In a French survey of 134 nursing homes, smelly urine was one of the reasons given for about 3 in 10 treated urine infections.

Smell and colour are poor guides on their own. In a small US study of 97 wet pads, judging by smell disagreed with urine tests about 1 time in 3.

In a larger US nursing home study of residents already suspected of infection, a change in colour, smell or visible blood raised the chance of lab signs of infection only a little: about 47 in 100 against 31 in 100. Those lab signs are common in residents with no infection at all.

Changes in smell or colour often have other causes, such as not drinking enough.

Report new pain or burning passing urine, new urgency or leaking, tummy or side pain, visible blood, or fever. And if antibiotics are suggested for smell or colour alone, ask why.
captions.linkedin:
Many people, including care staff, take smelly or dark urine as a sign of infection. In a French survey of 444 treated urine infections in 134 nursing homes, smelly urine was one of the reasons given in about 3 in 10 and cloudy urine in about 2 in 10.

What does the evidence say?

In a small US study of 97 wet pads from nursing home residents, judging by smell disagreed with urine tests about 1 time in 3. The test was for bacteria, not for true infection.

In a larger US nursing home study of residents already suspected of infection, lab signs of infection were found in about 47 in 100 when the urine had changed colour, smell or showed blood, and in about 31 in 100 when it had not. So a change raised the chance a little. But those lab signs are common in residents with no infection.

Infection experts writing criteria for care homes say changes in colour or smell often happen without infection, for example when someone is not drinking enough. Their criteria look instead for new urinary symptoms: pain or burning passing urine; new or much worse urgency, frequency or leaking; pain low in the tummy or in the side; visible blood; or fever with any of these. (They wrote these for surveillance, not as a treatment rule, and people with a catheter or who can't report symptoms need separate judgement.)

Treating bacteria without symptoms has a cost. In care home trials it cleared bacteria more often but did not reduce deaths or complications, and caused more side effects such as diarrhoea, rash and thrush. US guidance adds that it drives resistant bacteria.

My position: nobody should be given antibiotics for smelly or dark urine alone. Report new symptoms promptly, and ask why if antibiotics are suggested for smell or colour.

posts.title: Once a day is one normal among many
posts.insight: Going once a day is a common bowel pattern but not a rule; most people are irregular, and a lasting change from your own pattern is what needs checking.
posts.angle: Relieves a common worry about daily frequency while naming the changes that need a GP.
posts.position_basis: empirical finding (population studies) plus guidance on when to see a GP

captions.x:
Going once a day is one common bowel pattern. It is far from a rule.

In a study of about 1,900 adults in East Bristol (1992), once a day was the most common pattern. But only 40 in 100 men and 33 in 100 women went on a regular daily cycle, and a third of the women went less often than daily.

In US and Swedish studies of adults up to about 70, nearly everyone with normal bowels went between 3 times a day and 3 times a week.

Constipation means hard stools, straining or not feeling empty a good part of the time. Missing a day is not constipation on its own.

See your GP about a change from your usual pattern that lasts, blood in your stool, or weight loss you can't explain. A simple stool test, called FIT, helps decide on further tests.
captions.linkedin:
Going once a day is one common bowel pattern. It is far from a rule.

In a study of about 1,900 adults in East Bristol, published in 1992, once a day was the most common pattern. But only 40 in 100 men and 33 in 100 women went on a regular daily cycle. A third of the women went less often than once a day. The authors summed it up: most people had irregular bowels.

Two later studies give a range. Among US adults who said their bowels were normal, 96 in 100 went somewhere between 3 times a week and 3 times a day. A Swedish study of healthy adults aged 18 to 70 found the same range for 98 in 100. In these studies age made little difference, though they did not cover people much over 70, or people in hospital or care homes, where illness, moving less and medicines change bowel habit.

Doctors call it constipation when problems such as hard or lumpy stools, straining, a feeling of not having emptied, or going fewer than 3 times a week happen a good part of the time. Occasional straining is common in healthy people.

What deserves a GP visit is a change. Go if you have a lasting change from your own usual pattern, blood from your back passage or in your stool, or weight loss you can't explain. UK specialist guidance recommends that GPs use a simple stool test, called FIT, to help decide who needs urgent bowel tests. A normal FIT result does not settle it if symptoms carry on: ongoing concern should still lead to referral.

Your own pattern is the useful comparison.

posts.title: Has the incontinence been assessed?
posts.insight: Incontinence is linked with moving into a care home, and carers often hold off asking for help; an assessment can look for causes such as medicines, constipation and difficulty reaching the toilet, though home treatments have thin evidence.
posts.angle: Ask for a continence assessment and a look at treatment, equipment and night-time help; respect the person's preferences and the carer's limits.
posts.position_basis: mixed: Thom link and carer interviews are empirical; asking for an assessment is judgement

captions.x:
Has anyone looked for the causes of your relative's incontinence?

In an older US study of about 6,000 people aged 65 and over, those whose incontinence was recorded by doctors were more likely to move into a nursing home, after allowing for age and other illnesses. That is a link. It does not show that treating incontinence prevents a move.

In UK interviews with 32 family carers of people with dementia, most held off asking professionals for help with incontinence, often until a crisis.

An assessment looks for things that can be changed: medicines such as water tablets and sedatives, constipation, and difficulty getting to the toilet. It can also cover equipment and help at night.

Research on help at home is thin, so it may or may not help. Ask your GP or nurse for a continence assessment.
captions.linkedin:
Has anyone looked for the causes of your relative's incontinence?

Incontinence often comes up when families are talking about care. In an older US study of about 6,000 people aged 65 and over, those whose incontinence was recorded by doctors were about twice as likely (women) and three times as likely (men) to move into a nursing home, after allowing for age and other illnesses. That is a link. It does not show that treating incontinence prevents a move.

Carers often carry it alone. In a UK interview study of 32 family carers of people with dementia, most said they held off asking professionals for help with incontinence, often until a crisis.

Specialists in older people's care advise that clinicians ask about continence, and that assessment looks for causes, usually with more than one professional involved. Some contributors can be looked for and changed:

1. Medicines, such as water tablets and sedatives.
2. Constipation. In one small study, treating it was followed by less urgency and frequency.
3. Difficulty getting to the toilet: distance, stairs, lighting, clothing.
4. Equipment and night-time help, such as a commode or bottle.

A fair warning: research on help at home is thin. A 2024 review found only seven trials, and a review in dementia found too little evidence to recommend any approach. An assessment may find something that helps. It may not.

Whatever the family decides, the person's own wishes and the carer's limits both count. Ask the GP or practice nurse for a continence assessment.
captions.bluesky:
Has anyone looked for the causes of your relative's incontinence?

An assessment checks medicines, constipation and the route to the toilet, and can cover equipment and night-time help.

Evidence on home treatments is thin, so it may or may not help. Ask your GP or practice nurse.
captions.threads:

In UK interviews, most family carers of people with dementia held off asking for help with incontinence, often until a crisis.

posts.title: Looking after your own pessary
posts.insight: In a UK trial, women taught to remove and replace their own pessary had no clear difference in quality of life from clinic care, reported fewer pessary problems, and self-management was likely good value.
posts.angle: Care that respects agency and saves clinic trips, with the exclusions stated and clinic care respected as a choice.
posts.position_basis: mixed: trial results are empirical; 'ask whether you can be taught' is judgement supported by the trial authors' conclusion

captions.x:
A pessary is a small device placed in the vagina to hold up the pelvic organs when they have dropped (prolapse). Many women have it changed in clinic every 6 months or so.

A UK trial at 21 NHS clinics tested another option. 340 women were randomly assigned either to learn to remove, clean and replace their own pessary, or to keep clinic care.

After 18 months there was no clear difference in quality of life, and the self-managing women reported fewer pessary problems. Sore or damaged vaginal skin was found in about 18 in 100 of them, against 27 in 100 in clinic care. Self-management was likely good value for the NHS.

The trial left out women who could not use their hands well enough, or whose memory problems meant they couldn't self-manage. Clinic care stays a good choice.

If you use a pessary and could manage it, ask whether you can be taught.
captions.linkedin:
A pessary is a small device placed in the vagina to hold up the pelvic organs when they have dropped, a condition called prolapse. Many women have it removed and changed in clinic, usually every 6 months.

The TOPSY trial, run at 21 NHS clinics, tested another option. 340 women were randomly assigned either to learn to remove, clean and replace their own pessary, or to keep having it done in clinic. The support was modest: a 30-minute teaching session, a leaflet, a phone call after 2 weeks and a helpline number.

After 18 months:

1. There was no clear difference in quality of life between the groups.
2. Women who looked after their own pessary reported fewer pessary problems, such as difficulty emptying the bladder or bowel. On examination, sore or damaged vaginal skin was found in about 18 in 100 of them, compared with about 27 in 100 in clinic care.
3. Self-management cost the NHS less, about £578 per woman against £728, and was likely good value for money.

About half the women answered again after 4 years. There was still no clear difference in quality of life, and self-management still looked like good value.

The limits need stating. Women in the trial were typically in their mid-60s. It did not include women who couldn't use their hands well enough to remove a pessary, women whose memory or thinking problems meant they couldn't self-manage, or women who needed teaching in a language other than English. About 1 in 5 women taught to self-manage went back to clinic care. Many women prefer clinic care, and that choice deserves respect.

The trial's authors conclude that women who can self-manage should be offered the choice. If you use a pessary, ask your clinic whether you can be taught.

posts.title: Every catheter needs a leaving date
posts.insight: Only half of people newly catheterised on UK district nursing caseloads had any removal plan; the discharge record should state why the catheter went in, when, and who will remove it or try without it.
posts.angle: Each service can assume the next owns removal; three written facts break that loop.
posts.position_basis: mixed: survey and guidance are empirical/official; 'an incomplete discharge' is judgement

captions.x:
Only half of 267 people with a newly placed urinary catheter on UK district nursing caseloads had any plan for taking it out. Between organisations, the share with a plan ranged from 20 in 100 to 96 in 100.

The longer a catheter stays in, the higher the infection risk.

National guidance for NHS hospitals in England (epic3) says the record should state why the catheter went in, when, how long it should stay and the planned removal date, and that nobody should leave hospital with a short-term catheter without a written plan.

Three lines on the discharge letter: reason, date inserted, and who will remove it or try without it, and when. Without them the discharge is incomplete.
captions.linkedin:
Only half of 267 people with a newly placed urinary catheter on UK district nursing caseloads had any plan for taking it out: a review date, a date to try without it, or a referral to district nurses, urology or a continence service. Between organisations, the share with a plan ranged from 20 in 100 to 96 in 100.

Why it counts: the longer a catheter stays in, the higher the risk of infection. Almost everyone with a catheter has bacteria in their urine within a month (bacteria are not the same as infection, but the risk rises with time).

National guidance for NHS hospitals in England (epic3, 2014) sets the standard. The record should state why the catheter went in, when, how long it is expected to stay and the planned removal date, with the need checked every day. Nobody should leave hospital, or move to another ward or service, with a short-term catheter unless a plan is written down. The person and their family should be told why it is there and when it will be reviewed.

Prompts work in hospital. In hospital studies, reminders or automatic stop orders about halved catheter infection rates and shortened catheter use by about 2.6 days per patient. Most were before-and-after studies, which can overstate benefit, and none tested discharge or home.

Some NHS services use a catheter passport that the person keeps. In the survey only about 1 in 8 had one; those who did more often had a removal plan (78 in 100 against 46 in 100), though that link does not show the passport made the difference.

My position: a catheter without a recorded reason and removal plan at discharge is an incomplete discharge. Write the reason, the date inserted, and who will remove it or try without it, and when.

posts.title: From the chair to the toilet
posts.insight: Some leaks happen because getting to or using the toilet is hard; checking the route from chair to seat, day and night, finds practical things to change.
posts.angle: A continence assessment should include watching the route to the toilet; the checklist is practical judgement, not trial-tested.
posts.position_basis: mixed: mobility and environment as contributors and the falls links are empirical; the checklist is practical judgement

captions.x:
Getting to the toilet in time needs more than a bladder. It needs standing up, walking, opening a door, undoing clothes and sitting down.

Some leaks happen because one of those steps is hard: slow walking, memory problems, or the route and room itself.

Rushing carries its own risk. In a US study of about 6,000 older women, leaking with urgency at least weekly was linked with more falls and fractures over three years. Getting up at night to pass urine is also linked with a somewhat higher risk of falls. Both are links, not proof of cause.

Things worth checking: chair height, a walking aid within reach, a clear and lit route, clothes that open easily, and a commode or bottle at night. None is trial-tested, but each is cheap to look at.

Watching someone get from their chair to the toilet is part of a continence assessment.

This account posts practical care like this, with the evidence attached.
captions.linkedin:
Getting to the toilet in time needs more than a bladder. It needs standing up, walking, opening a door, finding the toilet, undoing clothes and sitting down.

Some leaks happen because getting to the toilet, or using it, is hard: slow walking, memory problems, or the route and the room themselves.

Rushing has its own risks. In a US study of about 6,000 older women, leaking with urgency at least weekly was linked with more falls and fractures over three years; leaking on coughing was not. Rushing to the toilet is one suggested explanation, not an established one. Getting up at night to pass urine is also linked with a somewhat higher risk of falls, and whether it causes them is uncertain.

A practical check, from chair to seat:

1. Can you stand from the chair easily, or is it too low?
2. Is the walking aid within reach?
3. Is the route clear and lit, including at night?
4. Does the door open easily, and is the toilet easy to find?
5. Do clothes undo quickly?
6. Is there a raised seat or rail if needed, and a commode or bottle for night?

None of these has been tested one by one in trials. They are things to check, and several are cheap.

My position: watching someone get from their chair or bed to the toilet belongs in every continence assessment of an older person. Therapists, nurses and families can all do it.

More posts in the Care that works series take one practical problem at a time.

posts.title: The bowel leakage people rarely mention
posts.insight: Accidental bowel leakage becomes more common with age, often has treatable causes, and in US surveys only about 1 in 3 people with it had talked to a doctor.
posts.angle: Gives the reader words to raise it and what a GP or nurse can check and offer.
posts.position_basis: mixed: prevalence and care-seeking are empirical; 'worth raising' is judgement

captions.x:
'I've had some accidents with my bowels' is a sentence your GP or practice nurse can act on.

Bowel leakage becomes more common with age. In a US national survey of adults living at home, about 3 in 100 people in their 20s reported any leakage in the past month, rising to about 15 in 100 of those aged 70 and over.

In two US surveys, only about 1 in 3 people with leakage had ever talked to a doctor about it.

Loose stools and constipation with leakage around hard stool are common causes, and both can be treated. First steps include advice on food, fibre and drinks, a regular toilet routine, a fibre supplement or a medicine that firms up stools, and pelvic floor exercises. If these don't help enough, there are further tests and treatments.

You can use the words 'bowel accidents'. Many people prefer them.
captions.linkedin:
"I've had some accidents with my bowels" is a sentence your GP or practice nurse can act on.

Bowel leakage becomes more common with age. In a US national survey of adults living at home in 2005 to 2006, about 3 in 100 people in their 20s reported any leakage in the past month, including small amounts of liquid or mucus. Among those aged 70 and over it was about 15 in 100, roughly 1 in 7. People in care homes were not included.

Few people raise it. In two US surveys, one of clinic patients in the 1990s and one of women aged 45 and over, only about 1 in 3 people with leakage had ever talked to a doctor about it. In the survey of women, 7 in 10 preferred the words "accidental bowel leakage" to "faecal incontinence". European guidance tells doctors and nurses to ask about it directly, using words like "accidents".

What a GP or nurse will ask about: your usual bowel pattern, because loose stools, and constipation with leakage around hard stool, are common causes that can be treated. Women are asked about childbirth, and anyone about past surgery near the back passage. A gentle examination checks the muscle and looks for hard stool.

First steps they can offer:

1. Advice on food, fibre and drinks, and a regular toilet routine.
2. A fibre supplement, or a medicine that firms up loose stools, such as loperamide (which can cause constipation).
3. Pelvic floor exercises.
4. Pads and skin care.

The evidence for each step is modest, and in trials advice alone did about as well as exercises. Many people improve. If first steps don't help enough, there are further tests and treatments.

If this is you, one sentence starts it.

posts.title: For men, consider a sheath before a catheter
posts.insight: For men who need urine collected but can empty their bladder, a sheath avoids a tube in the bladder; in a small trial it was more comfortable, with a composite outcome driven by bacteriuria.
posts.angle: An under-used, less invasive option for men without retention, with its evidence stated at its true strength.
posts.position_basis: mixed: trial and CDC guidance are empirical/official; 'consider a sheath first' is clinical judgement

captions.x:
For a man who leaks but can empty his bladder, a sheath collects urine outside the body, with no tube into the bladder.

In a US trial, 75 men in hospital (average age about 73) were randomly given a sheath or an indwelling catheter. Men found the sheath more comfortable and less painful.

A composite outcome, driven by bacteria found on daily urine tests, was lower with the sheath after adjustment; without adjustment the difference was not clear. Similar shares of men had any event (44 vs 49 in 100). The trial was small and single-site.

US guidance (CDC) suggests considering a sheath for cooperative men without retention or blockage. A sheath needs the right size, firm but not tight, changed daily, skin checked.

Consider a sheath before a catheter.
captions.linkedin:
For a man who leaks but can empty his bladder, a sheath collects urine outside the body, with no tube into the bladder.

The best trial is small. In a US veterans' hospital in the late 1990s, 75 men (average age about 73) who needed urine collected but had no retention were randomly given either a sheath or an indwelling catheter.

What it showed:

1. Men given a sheath were more likely to say it was comfortable and not painful. There was no difference in restriction of movement, embarrassment or inconvenience.
2. A composite outcome (bacteria in the urine, symptomatic infection or death) came out lower with the sheath after the researchers allowed for differences between groups. Without that adjustment the difference was not clear. The outcome was driven by bacteria found on daily urine testing; symptomatic infections and deaths were few. Similar shares of men had at least one event: 44 in 100 with a sheath, 49 in 100 with a catheter.
3. In a subgroup analysis the difference was larger in men without dementia, though the groups were small.

US infection control guidance (CDC, 2009) suggests considering a sheath instead of an indwelling catheter in men who can cooperate and have no retention or blockage. It is a weaker, Category II recommendation.

A sheath needs care too. A UK nursing review advises the right size, fitted firmly but not tightly, changed daily, with the skin checked regularly. Problems are usually minor, such as sore or damp skin, but a badly sized sheath can rarely cut off blood flow.

My position: for men without retention who need urine collected, a sheath should be considered before an indwelling catheter.
